idea: The world moves in patterns. When you visit a webpage, the page you land on nudges where you'll go next. When you speak, each word you just said constrains which word makes sense to say next. When you buy something, that choice shapes what you're likely to want later. This is not magic — it's just that the recent past leaves traces that point toward the immediate future. The core idea of sequential prediction is to build a model that learns these traces. You feed it a fragment of history — the last few pages visited, the last few words spoken, the last few items clicked — and ask it to bet on what comes next. The model doesn't need perfect knowledge of everything that ever happened. It only needs to capture the local dependencies, the short chains of cause-and-effect, that actually determine the next step. This is why sequential models are so powerful: they work with limited, realistic information rather than requiring a complete omniscient view.
why: Sequential prediction works because the world is not random, and crucially, it is locally non-random. The last three words in a sentence genuinely constrain which word can come fourth — not with certainty, but with enough probability that a model trained on examples can learn the pattern. The same holds for user behavior, event sequences, and time series: the immediate past really does make some futures more likely than others. The guarantee is conditional, not absolute. Given your last five purchases, the next purchase is more predictable than if we guessed with no history at all. Given the traffic flow at this intersection in the last ten minutes, the flow a few minutes from now has real statistical weight toward one outcome. This only breaks when the system is chaotic or adversarial — when noise dominates the signal, or when the pattern changes so fast that yesterday's behavior no longer applies. But in most real domains, whether it's user behavior, language, or physical systems, there is a buried regularity that sequential models can extract.
dots: The 63 papers in this group all lean on the same thread, but from wildly different angles. Recommendation systems (VK-LSVD, SEAR, Hyena Operator) predict the next item by learning from sequences of past clicks and purchases. Conversational systems (ES-MemEval, Swen, HingeMem) predict the next action or utterance by tracking dialogue history and user state. Time-series forecasting papers (MIGC-CMamba, Time-TK, RadioAR) predict the next value in a sensor stream or traffic count. Knowledge tracing (Leveraging LLM and Multiscale Knowledge States) predicts whether a student will solve the next problem by learning from their error trajectory. Even molecular generation (Graph Diffusion Evolution Model) is sequential: build the molecule step by step, predicting each new atom given the partial structure so far. The move is identical under each label: extract structure from ordered events, learn the conditional probabilities, and use them to forecast the next step. News recommendation (ONeRec, Real-Time Trend Prediction) predicts which article a user will engage with next by learning from their interest drift. Energy management (Statistical Analysis of 12V Power Load) predicts battery demand from power-load history. Suicide risk modeling (Suicide Risk Prediction) tracks emotional state trajectory to predict future risk. Even cryptocurrency arbitrage (Analysis of CEX-DEX Arbitrage) uses hidden state transitions to predict profitable moments. The single idea wears 63 different costumes, but in each case, the system is learning: past events carry information about the future, and that information can be extracted and acted on.
picture: Imagine standing at the top of a winding mountain path. You cannot see the whole path ahead, but you can see the last fifty meters behind you and sense the direction and steepness where you stand. That local information is enough to make a reasonable guess about where the path goes for the next few meters — it rarely makes sharp reversals, and gravity pulls certain ways. That's sequential prediction. You don't need to know the entire route from mountain base to peak. You just need to learn the local patterns that unfold: curves, climbs, switchbacks. Feed those patterns enough examples, and you can navigate forward one step at a time with surprising accuracy, even when the full landscape is unknown.
